title: The Mirror And The Light - review
transcript: hello and welcome to one-minute theater reviews i'm paul seven lewis this is the gilgood theater and i'm here for the world premiere of the mirror and the light following the royal shakespeare company's outstanding stage versions of the first two books of hillary mantell's trilogy we now arrive at the final volume the mirror and the light so did it reach the heights or fall from grace now just in case you don't know your history or haven't read the book we begin with thomas cromwell in prison his fate already sealed we see who his enemies are and who among his allies has betrayed him the prison set is dark and foreboding with high steely grey walls designed by christopher auram then we go back in time to when cromwell was still riding high and we realized the court is almost identical to the prison even the king is trapped by what is required of his position and the rest of prisoners to his royal whims the story of cromwell's fall plays out and is more not less tense for our knowing what awaits him we see the fragility of his power we see his own awareness of his vulnerability well that's the one minute review but keep watching for more about the mirror and the light it's important to say that this is not a simple adaptation of a novel it's as if writers hillary mantell and ben miles have taken the same story of cromwell and written a play about it so we're not inside cromwell's head as in the book but rather witnessing this central character's interaction with those around him showing how others see him and how he works the court in some ways it feels shakespearean and jeremy herron's production has the feel of a traditional production of one of his history plays everyone looking like they've stepped out of a painting by hans holbein the language while not as poetic has an elizabethan style but also it has pace and a natural feel the resemblance to modern day politics or even office politics in the mirror and the light is striking cromwell hated by his fellow councillors and by the people is entirely dependent on the goodwill of the king years ago british prime minister harold macmillan said that politicians feared events and so it proves for cromwell a mishandled northern rebellion the death of jane seymour a disastrous marriage for the king to anne of cleves and the king begins to have less faith in his right-hand man and that's all his enemies need chief of witch is the duke of norfolk played by nicholas wooderson as a little weasel of a man and he takes every opportunity to bring about cromwell's downfall and cromwell is always there or in at least in the other's thoughts he's not exactly a good man in fact actually he's a greedy manipulator but he comes across as honorable at least by the standards of the day and compassionate for example to princess mary in a way that few of the others seem to be ben miles performance as this complex man laughing worrying macho submissive his eyes constantly flitting around the room is a tour de force and he's complimented by nathaniel parker's henry the mirror in the light of the title who in fact is a capricious child in an oversized man's body self-indulgent self-pitying lonely a telling moment sees him alone feeling the cold desperate for the warmth of the fire but the cast of 24 this royal shakespeare company production has an epic feel and it's a well-chosen diverse cast who are a complement to the rsc's casting director helena palmer melissa allen reveals the steal in mary tudor you can see bloody mary waiting to burst out geoffrey lum as thomas risley and leo wan as richard reisch make you recoil at their sliminess uh tariq janata's cromwell's son gregory has a bright presence and jordan kowami was moving as cromwell's ally ray sadler desperate to save him without offending the king matthew pigeon's double act as the friendly ambassador eustach and the vicious bishop gardner is impressive inevitably death hangs over this evening the ghost of cromwell's old mentor cardinal woolsey played by a jolly tony turner is always around as is thomas's influential father influential on thomas i mean played with a spitting nastiness by liam smith now i'm sorry if i've made the evening sound grim because it's actually leveled with a great deal of humor paul adayfor brings comedy to cromwell's faithful french servant christoph a nicholas bolton is a tigger-like duke of suffolk a friend to cromwell in the sense of with friends like these who needs enemies and joe herbert has some great cynical one-liners as lady rashford olivia marcus is a sympathetic innocent jane with possibly the funniest moment of the evening when she complains to cromwell and some of the ladies about henry's unreasonable demands which an embarrassed thomas assuming them to be sexual tries to coax out over exactly what they are only to discover that she's referring to the king wanting her to ride with him to inspect the fortifications at dover after the roller coaster of events leading to cromwell's arrest the ending is somewhat downbeat and this is partly because cromwell accepts his fate with dignity and despite a dramatic beheading orchestrated by illusionist ben hart it's a climax that didn't leave me quite as shocked or drained as i expected nevertheless i give the mirror and the light four stars i hope you found this review useful and if you want to be the first to know about my future reviews please subscribe to this channel and if you'd like to read my reviews go to oneminutetheatrereviews.co.uk thank you for watching you
